name: Glutathione (IV)

lead: IV glutathione is the injected form of a natural antioxidant, offered in some clinics to lighten skin and even out tone. The basis is lab work showing glutathione can interfere with melanin production.

Glutathione is proposed to inhibit tyrosinase, the enzyme that makes melanin, and to shift pigment toward a lighter type. Dermatology reviews report that no rigorous trials establish that the intravenous route lightens skin and that standard dosing does not exist; oral and topical forms have small studies with variable results.

paras: It is given as a series of clinic drips, sometimes alongside other whitening treatments, with results judged over weeks to months. Use for cosmetic lightening is off-label.

Reviews associate IV use for lightening with anaphylaxis and liver toxicity concerns, and the Philippine FDA has acted on adverse-effect reports. A 2018 review did not suggest the IV route for skin lightening.

social.title: Does Glutathione Help Acne Marks and Pigmentation? The Science of PIH Explained

angle.text: Glutathione drips are offered in some clinics for lighter, more even skin. The idea comes from lab findings that glutathione inhibits tyrosinase and shifts melanin toward a lighter type. Reviews report limited clinical evidence for the intravenous route.

lead: Glutathione is a small antioxidant tripeptide that cells make naturally; intravenous (IV) glutathione is the injected form that is promoted in some countries and cosmetic clinics as a systemic skin-lightening treatment [1]. Proponents of the practice point to laboratory findings that glutathione can inhibit the enzyme tyrosinase and shift melanin production from the darker eumelanin toward the lighter pheomelanin [1].

Dermatology reviews report that there is a gap between the popularity of IV glutathione for skin lightening and the evidence behind it. A 2016 review stated that no evidence proves the efficacy of IV injections for this purpose and noted that adverse effects led the Philippine Food and Drug Administration to take regulatory action [1]. A 2018 review of systemic lightening treatments did not suggest IV glutathione because of the risk of adverse events, and a 2025 narrative review linked it to anaphylaxis and liver toxicity concerns, with no standardized dosing.
infobox: Glutathione, a tripeptide of glutamate, cysteine and glycine [1]

paras: IV glutathione is used or marketed to lighten overall skin tone and reduce pigmentation, and is described as widely used for this in some ethnic populations [1]. Reviews describe oral, topical and parenteral forms, with the IV form said to act more rapidly but carrying the most safety concerns. Commentary in medical journals has debated the ethics and safety of skin-lightening injections.

Outside cosmetics, IV glutathione has been tested in small clinical studies for other conditions, including a placebo-controlled pilot trial in Parkinson's disease [2], an earlier open trial in early Parkinson's disease [3], prevention of kidney oxidative stress after coronary angiography, chemotherapy-related neurotoxicity  and leg circulation in peripheral arterial disease [4]. These studies concern other conditions and do not address skin lightening.

For oral glutathione, a 2025 narrative review reported significant but variable decreases in melanin, and for topical forms a good level of melanin reduction with varying durability. A 2025 systematic review of topical glutathione found only five eligible clinical trials, with some suggesting improvement in hyperpigmentation.

For the intravenous route, reviewers describe rapid action in some reports but report an absence of rigorous trials, a lack of standardized dosing and an evidence base that does not establish long-term efficacy [1].

No clinical trial of intravenous glutathione for skin lightening is listed among the sources reviewed. Reviews of skin lightening describe human studies of oral and topical glutathione, including five trials of topical glutathione in a 2025 systematic review, and report no rigorous evidence for the IV route [1]. IV glutathione has been tested in small trials for unrelated conditions such as Parkinson's disease [2][3] and contrast-related kidney stress.

Case reports and reviews associate IV glutathione given for skin lightening with serious events including anaphylaxis and liver toxicity, and clinicians writing in medical journals have called the safety data inadequate. The Philippine FDA acted on adverse-effect reports [1], and a 2018 review advised against the IV route for lightening.

A 2025 pharmacokinetic modeling review argued that IV glutathione produces non-physiological plasma concentrations that could cause reductive stress, contrasting it with ozone therapy; this is a theoretical analysis rather than a clinical trial.

Glutathione is the most abundant non-protein thiol inside animal cells and acts as an antioxidant that recycles between reduced and oxidized forms [5]. Its proposed lightening effect is attributed to direct and indirect inhibition of tyrosinase and a switch from eumelanin to pheomelanin production [1]. Oral glutathione is described as poorly absorbed because digestive enzymes break it down, which is one reason injections are discussed [5].

Reviews characterize skin lightening with glutathione as an ethically contested practice in some societies, and one review suggested that promotion by pharma-cosmeceutical companies contributes to its popularity [1].
